item.title: Thoughts About Entropy and Objectives
item.description: A bunch of Reinforcement Learning Pre-Training (RLPT) papers have come out recently. They're cool. They even work kinda mostly. They can improve benchmark scores. So, like, probably there's gotta be something there. It's doing something. Unfortunately, nobody seems to be in agreement on what they are doing or why. Here's my understanding of the problem, and a take on a path forward.

item.title: A Treatise On ML Data Infrastructure

item.title: Prompting LLMs and Humans
item.description: Often you ask questions because you want to hear the other party's opinion. There are other reasons you may purposefully ask a leading question, but let's focus on the "soliciting opinions" case. Human or AI, you seek their perspective because it has value to you. You genuinely want to know. But when you phrase a question, you shape the answer you get. Every word matters. The context you provide, the tone you use, the assumptions you embed, etc. It all influences the response you get.

item.title: LLM Code Optimization
item.description: It's long been assumed that for most programmers writing hardware-optimized code is too hard. Few know, or want to know, how to exploit memory hierarchies, NUMA nodes, vector instructions, stop registers from spilling, or exploit the full memory bandwidth of the CPU. This is tragic. In the age of LLMs and tooling, we should expect more from our software and our hardware.

item.title: Hyperparameter Heuristics
item.description: Suppose you've invented a new neural architecture, or optimizer, or whatever, and you want to scale it up. You have 100 million dollars to do this with, and you want to train the best model you possibly can with that budget. But how should you choose your hyperparameters? There's no existing literature on your methods! Who knows what settings are optimal, and if you guess wrong, you're out a cool 100m.

item.title: The Craziest Bug I Have Ever Witnessed
item.description: I thought I had seen it all. Nah. Not even close. Julia has a feature where you can report bugs and crashes from the command line. You just run your program with julia --bug-report=rr, and it sends a crash report plus an rr trace of the process to our servers for us to take a look at. Sometimes we get some crazy stuff. This is in fact not the first time that someone from the Julia team has found something crazy in a crash dump. Keno Fischer wrote a similar (and substantially more detailed)...

item.title: How to Write a Compiler Without Going Insane
Safety and Correctness
item.description: Software safety is a lofty, but poorly defined goal. Everybody has their own opinion about how to achieve "safety" in software. However, nobody really seems to be able to define what that means.
